messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 33-year-old prosecutor from North America who has been struggling with PTSD following an act of terrorism that he witnessed. Married and dedicated to his work, David's life took a drastic turn after the traumatic event. The incident occurred during a routine court appearance when a bomb exploded in the courthouse, resulting in several casualties. Since then, every day feels like a struggle. David reports feeling extremely tired and exhausted most days. This fatigue is often triggered by seemingly mundane experiences, such as walking through an area where he catches a whiff of alcohol or hearing loud bangs that echo through his apartment building. These triggers are deeply intertwined with the trauma he experienced, making it nearly impossible for him to feel safe in environments that once seemed ordinary. The event itself remains vivid and real to David, even when he tries to recount what happened. He cannot tell a clear story of the sequence of events; instead, the memories of the bomb exploding and the chaos that followed feel more real and immediate than any other memory. It's as though the explosion happens all over again every time he closes his eyes or hears something that reminds him of the sound. David is haunted by the notion that he failed to protect others during the incident. He had been working in the courtroom when it happened, and even now, he feels an intense sense of guilt for not having done more to prevent the catastrophe. This constant self-blame has made him distrustful of everyone around him; he finds himself questioning whether people are truly what they seem to be. These negative appraisals have only deepened his emotional turmoil, making it harder for him to process and make sense of the traumatic event. David’s fragmented memories exacerbate these feelings of guilt and mistrust. He struggles with the idea that if he had acted differently or been more vigilant, perhaps things would have turned out differently. The vividness and immediacy of the memories keep his trauma alive in a way that continually reinforces his negative beliefs about himself and others. His occupation as a prosecutor has also taken a toll. The courtroom environment, once the center of his professional life, now triggers intense anxiety. David avoids cases that involve explosions or acts of violence. Even simple interactions with colleagues who were present during the event can lead to a breakdown in concentration and productivity. He often finds himself feeling exhausted after court appearances, as if he has relived the trauma all over again. The fatigue and exhaustion extend beyond his professional life into his marriage. David’s wife has noticed changes in him but struggles to understand what is happening beneath the surface. The combination of guilt and mistrust has made it difficult for him to open up about his experiences, leading to a sense of isolation even within his close relationship. David’s journey towards seeking help was gradual. He realized that his symptoms were not just fleeting distress but deeply ingrained patterns of thought and behavior. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never be able to forgive himself or reconnect with others in any meaningful way. Despite this, he is hopeful that through therapy, he can begin to process his experiences and find a path towards healing. In the end, David's story is one of resilience amidst overwhelming trauma. He has come to believe that understanding and addressing the interplay between his triggers, memories, and negative appraisals will be key in reclaiming his life from the shadows cast by the traumatic event.
